extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and editors (sports writers, society page editors, make-up editors)
extracted.subtask_short: writing and editing society & sports pages
extracted.subtask_description: Practical newsroom guidance for producing sports and society pages: story structure, sourcing, copy management, page makeup, photographs, and reader/audience considerations. Aimed at day-to-day reporters and desk editors responsible for these newspaper sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe the paper's style sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the style sheet dictates is to be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere strictly to the newspaper's established style rules when preparing copy; deviations force typesetters/makeup to refigure spacing and layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect linotyper/box-score constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting box scores is hard work; to ask him to set a box score containing one more column than usual demands that he refigure each and every space adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't add nonstandard columns or formatting to box scores; extra columns double the linotyper's time and complicate page make-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story structure — Block 1: The lead
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead: statement of the result of the most interesting fight, with the five Ws and with a compact account of the decisive moments of the fight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include who/what/where/when/why and a concise description of the decisive moments. Example lead: 'Sammy Frayne... knocked out Terrier Ryan... in the sixth round...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Story structure — Block 2: The secondary lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary lead: report results of other fights (or secondary events) and brief notable facts about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concise results and salient facts for the secondary items that follow the main lead; e.g., mention other winners, rounds, weights, and notable occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story structure — Block 3: The catch-all
rubrics_metrics.description: The catch-all: miscellaneous announcements such as next week's program or other notices not part of the lead or secondary lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this block for forward-looking or miscellaneous information (e.g., manager announcements, upcoming matches) that don't fit in immediate results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story structure — Block 4: Elaboration of the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaboration of the lead, following the sequence of action indicated in the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand the lead by recounting the action in sequence (round-by-round or chronological detail) to give readers fuller understanding of how the result occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story structure — Block 5: Elaboration of the secondary lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaboration of the secondary lead, with each fight described in the sequence of its listing in the secondary lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each item in the secondary lead, provide a short narrative in the same order as listed, giving readers consistent structure and predictable flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justified speculation only
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculation based upon long and expert observation is acceptable; speculation by an inexperienced reporter is unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do 'dope writing' (predictions/forecasts) only when grounded in substantial observation and recognized authority; avoid fanciful predictions from casual observation (Burt example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of slang — be expert and economical
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing said heretofore indicts the intelligent use of slang. Slang by an expert is one of the beauties of English; slang by an imitator is barbaric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using slang, ensure it feels natural and authored by someone who understands it; avoid forced or trendy phrasing that requires readers to 'stop and decode' and thus loses general readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overused/new phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: New phrasing adopted widely is often worked to death in a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on novelty catch-phrases that will quickly wear out; seek freshness but avoid faddish repetition across the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fight monotony & devise new story themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Fighting the monotony of sports routine is a matter of devising new story themes as well as varying vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When routine events become soporific, find a fresh angle/peg to hang the story on (metaphor, theme, human interest) rather than repeating the same descriptive patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid too much technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much technical writing limits the number of readers; explain terms familiar only to fans compactly for casual readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define or briefly explain specialized terms (e.g., 'seeded draw', formations) so casual readers can follow; fans will tolerate compact explanations and general readers will appreciate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not imitate another writer's style
rubrics_metrics.description: If a new reporter borrows an admired writer's style, it loses in the process; he hasn't tinkered with that method and will misuse it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate your own voice; copying a practiced style often fails and reduces effectiveness (analogy: learning motorcycle then driving trailer-truck).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports column principle — variety
rubrics_metrics.description: The column must not be all baseball, all golf, or all anything else; it must be diversified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include multiple sports/topics (seasonal interests like duck hunting during football season) to retain a broad readership rather than appealing only to niche fans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports column principle — tolerance (tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disagree vigorously but avoid branding the other fellow as a 'murkywit' — cheap personal attacks cheapen the column and stir resentment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain robust critique without personal vilification; consider community impact (example of college-town columnist embarrassing himself).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand society-page audience differences
rubrics_metrics.description: The little-city and the big-city society pages are greatly different; metropolitan page tells about the socially elect, small-city page caters to ordinary housewives/high-school girls/store clerks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor content to the paper's readership: metropolitan pages focus on 'genuine society' and the unusual; small-city pages emphasize local names and everyday activities that readers care about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the society page as a valuable circulation tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The society page is one of the most attentively read in the entire paper and an important factor in gaining and holding circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't dismiss personal/club notices as trivial; they create reader loyalty because people like to see themselves and acquaintances mentioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify every marital/engagement announcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Inez has it as an ironclad, unalterable rule that every marital tiding must be verified before it goes into the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never publish wedding/engagement news on rumor or single-source hearsay; verification prevents embarrassment/hoaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get names and addresses correctly — never guess
rubrics_metrics.description: Over the wire 'Burpee' can sound completely like 'Durkee.' She never guesses at an unfamiliar name; she looks it up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm spelling and addresses by checking records or calling back; accuracy in names is essential to credibility and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be systematic — keep a future book
rubrics_metrics.description: Inez keeps a future book with the full meticulousness of the most fussy city editor; without it she will overlook many important happenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record recurring meetings, special events and dates; use the future book to prepare time copy ahead of events and avoid forgetting notable items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate publicity chairmen and prompt reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Inez welcomes the publicity chairmen from the clubs and cajoles them into making their reports more promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build diplomatic relationships with club publicity officers to obtain timely info; promptness improves freshness and placement of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and manage a wide contact list of 'in-the-know' sources
rubrics_metrics.description: She builds a list of women 'in the know' to whom she telephones frequently; if her list has 150 or 200 names she need call Mrs. Windham only once every two or three weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a large, rotating contact list so the personals column includes many names and avoids over-relying on a small set of contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use neighborhood 'gossips' as reporting auxiliaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Enlist a dozen or so neighborhood gossips as ex-officio reporters; often their only pay is a free copy of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit unpaid local informants for tips, but monitor their accuracy and remove those who prove unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make arrangements with service businesses for tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Make treaties with people whose business brings them in contact with women planning social happenings (beauty-parlor managers, florists, caterers, musicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer modest rewards (gift subscriptions, payments, mentions) for good tips; these contacts can provide advance knowledge of parties, engagements, and other newsworthy events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept inbound tips but control publicity grabbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many townspeople call or write with tidbits; some are modest informants, others are publicity grabbers who want mentions seven days a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Welcome reader-submitted items but limit repetitive mentions of space-hogs; ensure coverage remains deserved and balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare time copy (local and wire) to cover slow periods
rubrics_metrics.description: If ambitious, prepare a quantity of time copy, as usable Thursday as Monday; local time copy comes from the future book; wire copy via the telegraph editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a bank of evergreen local and syndicated (wire) features slugged for society use (e.g., 'Soc. Misc.') to fill the page when local news is thin; but periodically check and kill out-of-date pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularly inspect plug type and proofs to kill out-of-date copy
rubrics_metrics.description: She is careful to get proofs about once a fortnight, so that she can order killed any copy now out of date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review scheduled/time copy on a regular basis to avoid running seasonally or factually outdated stories (example: summer vacation copy running in winter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain picture and cut files comprehensively
rubrics_metrics.description: She wants a photograph or a cut of every woman in town who might by any chance be worth mentioning on the society page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep an organized photo/cut archive to supply images for stories; avoid repeating the same photo for a woman within a week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire three standard photos for prominent women
rubrics_metrics.description: For the more prominent women, try for three pictures: one a full-face view, one facing right, and the third facing left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing three orientations helps makeup place photos in different layouts without cropping or awkward directionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace outdated cuts to avoid offending subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Inez keeps the department's engraving bill high by replacing cuts five or ten years old with more modern pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update images periodically so subjects are not shown in old hairstyles or fashions that could alienate them from the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jealousies by consistent omission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: To sidestep jealousies, omit all similar minor groups (e.g., all sewing circles) rather than favoring a few; exceptions only for notably special meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply uniform rules for which small organizations get full stories vs calendar listing to prevent perceived favoritism and backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish a complete club calendar for minor organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Print each day a 'club calendar' listing time, place, and topic of meetings for clubs too minor to have a separate story; make the calendar complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The club calendar provides modest publicity to many groups and reduces resentment; ensure accuracy and completeness to avoid anger from omitted clubs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help the make-up editor — get copy in early
rubrics_metrics.description: To get her copy in early. When the day is young, the linotypers howl for work. Her copy available then, it is set gladly and easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver early copy to secure typesetting priority, allow better planning, and avoid being labeled 'behind-time girl.' Early type enables effective page design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help the make-up editor — make copy fit the dummy space
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at the advertising 'dummy' and accept it as unalterable; if the dummy shows eighty-eight inches available for news, Inez doesn't try to smuggle an extra half-column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare copy to the space available; plan lengths to match ad layouts and avoid last-minute content overflow that forces clumsy make-up solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help the make-up editor — warn early of copy overflow
rubrics_metrics.description: If she cannot keep her copy down to the intended space, she tells the make-up editor promptly so he can reschedule the paper and give her extra space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide early warnings of excess copy so makeup can allocate facing-page space; lateness may relegate overflow to a distant page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help the make-up editor — provide a list of stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the make-up editor a list of her stories so he can check each off and know none was missed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A checklist helps prevent omissions; without it, late items may be lost or moved to unrelated pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help the make-up editor — supply stories long enough for headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide plenty of stories long enough to wear headlines; for each column of space, Inez should have at least two stories carrying headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines break up 'all-grey' pages; on dull days, combine short personals into grouped leads to create headline-bearing items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help the make-up editor — adjust pictures to the space
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust pictures to the space; scheduling two 2-column pictures side by side when advertising runs high on the page can make the make-up editor 'licked.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan photo sizes and placements to match ad shapes and avoid awkward touching of ads or off-column placements that complicate makeup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help the make-up editor — vary picture arrangements daily
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a different picture arrangement each day instead of everlastingly calling for two 2-column pictures, side by side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a repertoire of layouts (sample variations listed) to keep the page visually interesting and to give the make-up editor workable options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture arrangement sample variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample picture arrangements include: three 2-column cuts under a six-column caption; two 2-column pictures under a four-column caption; three 1 1/3-column pictures under a four-column caption; two 1 1/3-column pictures with 1/3-column stories beside them; one 2-column picture flanked by one-columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific arrangements illustrate how contrasts in picture and type width and white-space patches can create attractive page structures; choose arrangements appropriate to advertising constraints.
